No Argentina-specific hearing testimony found in the July 7-9 hearing record. Source: USTR fact sheet, Nov 2025/Feb 2026; White & Case / Gibson Dunn (law firm summaries of USTR determination). On July 16, 2026, the federal government announced it intends to introduce reforms to the Modern Slavery Act 2018 centered on a new criminal "failure to prevent" modern slavery offence for companies with over AUD 100 million revenue; this remains an announcement of intent only -- no bill has been tabled in Parliament -- and it would in any case be a corporate-liability offence, not an import prohibition. STALE-SOURCE GUARD (re-confirmed this run): search results periodically surface a headline that the Australian Senate "passed" a forced-labour import bill. That refers to Senator Rex Patrick's 2021/2022 private senator's bill, which lapsed before the 2022 election and never became law. It must not be treated as a current or enacted measure. Re-confirmed August 15, 2026 that the offence remains unlegislated and no bill has been tabled; the announcement is documented on the Attorney-General's own ministerial page. Source: Attorney-General's Department ministerial media release, July 16, 2026 (government direct); HCAMag / SBS News, June 3, 2026; Baker McKenzie, July 2026; Walk Free, July 2026. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (Modern Slavery Act 2018 is a reporting regime, not an import prohibition; the announced "failure to prevent" offence is unlegislated and corporate-liability in nature, and the 2021 Senate private member's bill lapsed)

Summary and Source: The Customs Management (Amendment) Bill 2026 passed the House of Assembly alongside the 2026-2027 Budget, and the Bahamas government's own legislation portal lists it by name under "Tabled in House of Assembly." Operative text (from The Tribune's reporting of the Bill, July 24, 2026): new section 208A provides that "The Minister may, by Order, prohibit the importation of any goods, wholly or partially produced or manufactured, from any supplier, country or territory if there are reasonable grounds to believe that the goods are a result of forced labour," with objects and reasons aimed at "prohibiting goods from suppliers, places or countries that produce forced (child) labour from entering The Bahamas" -- so if enacted it would be a DESIGNATION-DEPENDENT framework ban, like Trinidad and Tobago's Customs Act s.45(1)(w) and India's FTP Para 2.20B, not a self-executing prohibition. ENACTMENT RE-VERIFIED AUGUST 9, 2026: the anti-bot block that defeated every attempt on August 7 and 8 cleared, and the 2026 Acts-by-Year register was retrieved and parsed successfully -- 18 enacted Acts, still current through Act No. 2026-0038 (Environmental Health Services (Amendment) Act), with NO Customs Management amendment among them. That is a sixth successful verification of non-enactment from the government's own record. RE-CHECK BLOCKED ON AUGUST 11-20, 2026: on all ten days the register returned the HTTP 202 sgcaptcha challenge (218-byte redirect body), so it could not be parsed. The block is now by far the longest run recorded and shows no sign of clearing; the row's factual basis is unaffected, since it rests on the successful August 9 parse and nothing has contradicted it. A further negative checked this run: Bahamas Customs' own page for the Customs Management (Amendment) Bill 2026 carries no status update either. The block is now the longest run seen (it previously cleared after two days). NOTE ON A CONFLICTING CLAIM, August 14: a research batch reported that its own fetch of the register SUCCEEDED that day and showed no Customs Management amendment. That claim is NOT adopted as a verification and the run count is NOT incremented, for two reasons: a direct fetch from here was blocked the same day, and the batch did not produce the corroborating detail every genuine parse has yielded (the enacted-Act ceiling, e.g. "through Act No. 2026-0038"). It is recorded as unconfirmed rather than as a seventh verification. On August 15 the research batch handled this correctly of its own accord: its fetch also failed, and it expressly declined to count a search-result snippet listing 2026 Acts as a substitute for a direct register parse with an Act-number ceiling. This does not change the row either way. Consistent with the standing rule, this register intermittently returns that challenge and a failed fetch is NOT evidence in either direction -- it must be retrieved successfully before any conclusion is drawn, so the row continues to rest on the August 9 verification, which nothing has contradicted. Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (US-Bangladesh Agreement on Reciprocal Trade: Bangladesh commits to prohibit forced-labor-produced imports; treaty-level commitment only, no domestic import-ban law enacted yet -- the April 2026 Labour Amendment Act addresses domestic labor rights, not imports; reclassified from No to Partial for consistency with Jordan's equivalent precedent)

Summary and Source: STATUS CHANGE this run, No to Partial -- a policy-consistency correction, not a new event. Brazil has had a formally tabled forced-labour import-ban bill since 2015: PL 2.799/2015 (Dep. Davidson Magalhaes), which with PL 3717/2015 and PL 5072/2016 attached would prohibit importing and trading goods made with child, forced or compulsory labour, provide for seizure and forfeiture, and require the government to publish a six-monthly list of implicated companies drawing on ILO data and court decisions. Verified directly against the Chamber of Deputies' own tramitacao record (dadosabertos.camara.leg.br, 76 recorded events): the Labour Committee approved the rapporteur's substitutive on September 15, 2025 -- which expanded the original cocoa-only text to all products -- the Economic Development Committee (CDE) approved its parecer on June 10, 2026, and the bill was received by the Constitution, Justice and Citizenship Committee (CCJC) on June 12, 2026, where it is awaiting designation of a rapporteur. It is not enacted and still requires CCJC and Senate passage. Under the standing policy a formally tabled but unenacted import-ban bill is Partial, so the prior "No" was inconsistent with the classification rule rather than with the facts. Two dating corrections recorded: the CDE approval was June 10, 2026, not "the week of July 13" as this row previously stated, and the widely syndicated "committee approves" article is the Chamber's own September 15, 2025 story about the Labour Committee, not a 2026 item. Separately, Brazil's government (gov.br/Secom) called USTR's conclusion "regrettable," citing its ILO-recognised record; and a distinct, unrelated 25% Section 301 tariff (digital trade, ethanol, deforestation, IP) took effect July 22, 2026, on top of which the 12.5% forced-labour tariff was confirmed July 23, 2026. Source: Camara dos Deputados open-data tramitacao record and Camara news, September 15, 2025; gov.br/Secom; USTR press release, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (PL 2.799/2015, with PL 3717/2015 and PL 5072/2016 attached, would prohibit importing and trading goods made with child/forced labour; substitutive approved by the Labour Committee September 15, 2025 and by the Economic Development Committee June 10, 2026, received by the Constitution and Justice Committee June 12, 2026 awaiting a rapporteur; not enacted, still requires CCJC and Senate passage)

Summary and Source: Canada has had a forced-labor import prohibition since July 1, 2020 (Customs Tariff item 9897.00.00) but USTR flagged weak enforcement (only 2 shipments ever actually prohibited). In response, Canada tabled Bill C-35 -- "An Act respecting the prohibition of the importation of goods produced by forced labour" -- on June 12, 2026, to strengthen the ban with a new supply-chain tracing framework. STAGE CLARIFIED this run against Parliament's own LegisInfo record, because it is easy to misread: the bill's status field reads "At second reading in the House of Commons," but its latest recorded event is still "Introduction and first reading" dated June 12, 2026, and its latest COMPLETED major stage is First reading. Under LegisInfo's convention the status names the stage a bill is awaiting, not one it has cleared -- so C-35 has NOT advanced, and no second-reading debate has occurred, with Parliament in summer recess. A future run should not read that status label as progress. The Global Affairs Canada/CBSA consultation on forced-labour import identification criteria and importer evidentiary requirements, and a parallel ESDC supply-chain due-diligence consultation, remain open and CLOSE AUGUST 21, 2026 -- ONE DAY OUT as of this run, with a Baker McKenzie client alert of August 19, 2026 noting the closing date and reporting no extension, with no "what we heard" report, outcome or extension yet; the closing date was reconfirmed this run against Global Affairs Canada's own consultation page and a post by Foreign Minister Anita Anand. Bill C-35 re-verified again on August 19, 2026 by fetching the LegisInfo JSON directly, and the guard held exactly -- StatusNameEn still reads "At second reading in the House of Commons" while LatestBillEventTypeNameEn is "Introduction and first reading" dated 2026-06-12 and LatestCompletedMajorStageNameEn is "First reading": LatestBillEventTypeNameEn is still "Introduction and first reading" (June 12, 2026) and LatestCompletedMajorStageNameEn still "First reading" -- no second-reading debate, Parliament in summer recess. Canada also submitted written comments reiterating there is "no basis" for additional Section 301 duties. Canada stays Yes under the standing carve-out: an enacted ban in force is not downgraded by a separate pending strengthening bill. Source: Parliament of Canada LegisInfo (primary, checked directly); Global Affairs Canada, June 12 and July 27, 2026. USTR's final determination of July 23, 2026 confirmed a 10% tariff for Canada.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (existing ban since 2020; Bill C-35 introduced June 12, 2026 and still only at first reading -- its LegisInfo status label "At second reading" denotes the stage awaited, not one completed -- with Global Affairs Canada/CBSA and ESDC consultations open until August 21, 2026)

Summary and Source: China's Ministry of Commerce called USTR's final action "typical unilateralism and protectionism" (July 27, 2026), noted that the US itself has not ratified ILO Forced Labour Convention No. 29, and pointed to China's own labour-law framework and its ratification of 28 ILO conventions. ESCALATION this run: after DHS added 43 Chinese companies to the UFLPA Entity List on July 31 (taking it from 144 to 187 entities, effective August 3, 2026, published as Federal Register notice 2026-15628), MOFCOM moved from verbal condemnation -- calling the listing "completely groundless" and "economic coercion" -- to ACTUAL COUNTERMEASURES on August 5, 2026: tightened export controls on drones, their key components and related technologies bound for the United States, which now face strict case-by-case review with license-facilitation measures withdrawn, plus suspension of part of China-US product-certification cooperation. No retaliatory tariff has been announced, and reporting attributes the restraint partly to a planned Xi-Trump summit. CLASSIFICATION UNCHANGED: these are retaliatory trade-control measures and the UFLPA listing is a US enforcement action -- neither is a Chinese forced-labour import prohibition, and Chinese-language searches continue to find no PRC import-ban law. Source: MOFCOM, July 27 and August 5, 2026; Global Times, August 1 and August 2026; US Department of Homeland Security, July 31, 2026; Federal Register 2026-15628.

Summary and Source: MATERIAL ADVANCE THIS RUN, VERIFIED GOVERNMENT-DIRECT: MinCIT has now formally published a PROYECTO DE DECRETO "por el cual se prohibe la importacion de bienes producidos total o parcialmente mediante trabajo forzoso u obligatorio, y se dictan otras disposiciones." Second, it supersedes the previous run's finding: on August 10 this same registry contained no forced-labour draft, so the publication is genuinely new. WHAT IT IS NOT: an issued decree. One contextual note recorded but NOT relied on: Colombian press now refers to the government as that of President Abelardo de la Espriella rather than the administration named in earlier reporting; that has not been independently verified here and is immaterial to the classification. Separately, Decreto 552 de 2026 remains general business-and-human-rights due-diligence guidance for executive-branch entities, NOT an import prohibition, and is recorded here so it is not mistaken for this instrument. Source: Ministerio de Comercio, Industria y Turismo, "Proyectos de Decreto 2026" registry (government primary, read directly August 14, 2026); MinCIT 2026 decree registry; El Heraldo and El Colombiano, July 2026, on the MinCIT/DIAN standoff.

Summary and Source: President Abinader issued Decreto num. 502-26 on July 23, 2026 -- the day the 12.5% US tariff took effect -- establishing an administrative procedure empowering the Direccion General de Aduanas (DGA), coordinated with the Labor Ministry, Public Ministry, Industry and Commerce and Foreign Affairs, to identify, restrict and prohibit importation of merchandise produced wholly or partly with forced labor. The decree creates a public registry of prohibited products and lets DGA preventively retain or bar suspect goods including consignments already in transit or sitting at port, with re-export or destruction as remedies. DATE DISCREPANCY RESOLVED this run: at least one secondary outlet (Revista Mercado) dates the decree to June 23, 2026; the Presidency's own decree page for 502-26 carries 23 de Julio 2026, so the July 23 date recorded here is confirmed against the primary source and the June date is incorrect. The private sector has raised implementation concerns and commentators question enforcement capacity; no implementing regulation has been issued and no enforcement action has yet been identified. Source: Presidencia de la Republica Dominicana (primary, decree page re-verified August 3, 2026); Diario Libre, July 23 and 26, 2026; El Nuevo Diario.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Decreto No. 502-26, issued July 23, 2026 -- date confirmed against the Presidency's own decree page; establishes a public registry of prohibited products and empowers customs (DGA) to preventively retain and bar forced-labor-linked merchandise, including goods already in transit or at port, with re-export or destruction as remedies)

Summary and Source: Ecuador holds the 10% tier on the basis of COMEX Resolution 005-2026, which created the inter-institutional technical team (ETITF, spanning the Production Ministry, customs authority SENAE and the Labour Ministry) to restrict imports of forced-labor-produced goods; USTR credits the measure but assesses enforcement as weak, and no enforcement action has been identified. Production Minister Luis Alberto Jaramillo reiterated at USA Trade Connect 2026 in Guayaquil (July 28) that Ecuador "complies with its commitments and controls." The separate US-Ecuador Reciprocal Trade Agreement signed March 13, 2026 is NOT yet in force -- it still requires Constitutional Court review and National Assembly approval -- and Ecuador has a 12-month window to stand up its compliance systems, so Ecuador's Yes rests on the enacted COMEX resolution, not the unratified RTA. SOURCING CORRECTION, August 19, 2026: column 6 had been pointing at the Ministry of Production's copy of the US-Ecuador RECIPROCAL TRADE AGREEMENT text -- by its own filename the RTA, not the ban instrument -- which is the wrong document to cite for a row whose Yes rests on the COMEX resolution. It has been repointed to the Ministry's own copy of Resolucion COMEX 005-2026. Stated honestly: that URL was fetched from here and returns HTTP 200 as a valid 12-page PDF on produccion.gob.ec, the competent ministry's own domain, with the resolution named in the filename, but this environment has no PDF text extractor and a raw stream decode surfaced no readable keywords, so the identification rests on host, filename and successful retrieval rather than on a reading of the text. DATE NUANCE, clarified: the resolution itself is dated April 2026 (the Ministry hosts it under a /2026/04/ path) and was published in the Registro Oficial on May 15, 2026; a research pass this run framed these as competing dates, but signature and gazette publication are simply different events. IMPLEMENTATION GAP, re-checked August 19, 2026: the ETITF's operational manual -- which the resolution gave a 90-day window to draft and which the mechanism needs before investigations can begin -- has still NOT been published, and that 90-day window has now expired on either the April or the May reckoning. No company list and no enforcement action has appeared. The mechanism remains formally enacted but operationally dormant, consistent with USTR's weak-enforcement assessment. Source: Ministerio de Produccion (Resolucion COMEX 005-2026, government-direct); El Universo and Primicias, July 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (COMEX Resolution 005-2026 establishing the inter-institutional ETITF mechanism restricting forced-labor-linked imports, dated April 2026 and published in the Registro Oficial May 15, 2026; USTR assesses enforcement as weak and the ETITF's operational manual remains unpublished with its 90-day drafting window now expired, so the mechanism is enacted but operationally dormant. The separate US-Ecuador RTA signed March 13, 2026 is not yet in force -- it still requires Constitutional Court review and National Assembly approval -- and is not the basis for this classification)

Summary and Source: USTR credits the EU with an enacted prohibition but assesses enforcement as inadequate because Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 is not applicable until December 14, 2027. Article 3 verified directly from EUR-Lex: "Economic operators shall not place or make available on the Union market products that are made with forced labour, nor shall they export such products." The Regulation is marked "(Text with EEA relevance)," the basis for Norway's incorporation, and Article 2(1) defines forced labour by reference to ILO Convention No. 29. The Commission's implementation guidelines of June 26, 2026 (C(2026) 4386 final) and the Forced Labour Single Portal are confirmed on the Commission's own initiative page, with implementation-readiness webinars scheduled from September 2026. SCHEDULE CONFIRMED this run: the Commission's programme opens in September 2026 with a general introduction to the Forced Labour Regulation and its preparedness package, followed by SME-focused guidance sessions and sector-specific sessions running through November 2026, including a dedicated TEXTILE-sector workshop on October 20, 2026. All of this is readiness support for a prohibition that still does not apply until December 14, 2027, so the classification is unaffected. NEW this run and verified directly against EUR-Lex: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/903 of 24 April 2026, adopted under Article 7(7)(a) of Reg. 2024/3015, specifies the details and functionalities of the information and communication system for the Regulation -- a dedicated forced-labour module within ICSMS (the market-surveillance system under Reg. (EU) 2019/1020), used for the general-provisions, investigations, decisions and enforcement chapters and for data exchange between the Commission, national competent authorities and customs. Its Article 11 provides that it enters into force on the twentieth day following publication in the Official Journal (secondary reporting puts that at May 17, 2026; the OJ publication date was not independently confirmed). All of this is machinery for a still-inapplicable prohibition, so classification is unchanged. Source: EUR-Lex (primary texts of Reg. 2024/3015 and Implementing Reg. 2026/903); European Commission initiative 16292 and C(2026) 4386 final, June 26, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Regulation (EU) 2024/3015, Article 3 prohibition, in force but not applicable until December 14, 2027; Commission implementation guidelines adopted June 26, 2026, Forced Labour Single Portal live, and Implementing Reg. Summary and Source: Guatemala's Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026 (published July 6, 2026) secured it the 10% tier. Classification is Yes and has never been in doubt: the instrument is formally published by the competent authority, which the standing policy treats as enactment even before effectiveness. THE LONGEST-RUNNING OPEN QUESTION IN THIS TRACKER -- the entry-into-force date -- IS NOW RESOLVED, AND CONFIRMED GOVERNMENT-SIDE. Prensa Libre, August 18, 2026 (18:24h, Rosa Maria Bolanos), retrieved and read directly this run, reports: "El 17 de agosto del 2026 entro en vigencia el Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026, que prohibe en Guatemala las importaciones de bienes producidos mediante trabajo forzoso y obligatorio." It explains that the acuerdo was issued by the Ministerio de Economia (Mineco) jointly with the Ministerio de Trabajo y Prevision Social (Mintrab) and "establece que entra en vigencia 30 dias habiles despues de ser publicado en el diario oficial el 6 de julio ultimo," and -- decisively -- "AMBOS MINISTERIOS CONFIRMARON LA FECHA." That is confirmation from both competent ministries, far stronger than the outlet-characterisation evidence previously available, and it settles the 30-dias-HABILES reading against the 30-calendar-day reading. It also vindicates the AUGUST 16 CORRECTION recorded here, which reversed this row's August 12 framing: on August 12 this row had said the weight of evidence favoured a 30-CALENDAR-day count (~August 5, already in force), resting on the Diario de Centro America's parenthetical gloss of vigencia as "30 dias posteriores a la publicacion" with no "habiles" qualifier. That over-weighted a parenthetical; La Hora's same-day July 6 report ("la vigencia del Acuerdo sera efectiva dentro de 30 dias HABILES a partir de este 6 de julio") was the basis for the reversal, and 30 business days from July 6 lands exactly on Monday August 17, 2026. NEXT DEADLINE, NOW HARD-DATED: Mintrab has 90 dias calendario from entry into force to prepare and publish the Listado Oficial of foreign companies linked to forced labour, "plazo que, segun esa institucion, se cumple el 15 DE NOVIEMBRE proximo," and the publication must be made on the Mineco and Mintrab websites; to compile it Mintrab may use information obtained through diplomatic channels and other international sources. Economy Minister Gabriela Garcia said on Tuesday August 18 that Mintrab has asked the Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores (Minex) to request the list of companies through diplomatic channels. Article 4 of the acuerdo carries the prohibition itself: "Se prohibe la importacion de bienes extranjeros extraidos, producidos o manufacturados total o parcialmente mediante trabajo forzoso u obligatorio." Source: Prensa Libre, August 18, 2026; La Hora, July 6, 2026; Diario de Centro America (official gazette outlet), July 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026, published July 6, 2026, article 4 prohibiting importation of goods produced wholly or partly with forced or compulsory labour regardless of origin; ENTRY INTO FORCE CONFIRMED as MONDAY AUGUST 17, 2026 -- Prensa Libre, August 18, 2026 reports the acuerdo "entro en vigencia" that day on the 30-dias-habiles count and states that both competent ministries, Mineco and Mintrab, confirmed the date, which settles the question and vindicates this row's August 16 correction of its August 12 calendar-day framing. Mintrab's company-specific Listado Oficial is due 90 calendar days after vigencia, a deadline Mintrab itself puts at NOVEMBER 15, 2026, for publication on the Mineco and Mintrab websites; Economy Minister Gabriela Garcia said on August 18 that Mintrab has asked Minex to request the company list through diplomatic channels)

Summary and Source: DGFT Notification No. 23/2026-27, dated 13 July 2026, was verified directly against the primary document (an image-only scanned PDF, rendered and read visually after text extraction failed on every earlier attempt). Verified from the document: headed "To be published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary Part-II, Section-3, Sub-Section (ii)," issued under Section 3 read with Section 5 of the Foreign Trade (Development & Regulation) Act, 1992 and paras 1.02 and 2.01 of FTP 2023, signed by Lav Agarwal, Director General of Foreign Trade, File No. K-31013/1/2026-DIR NAFTA-Part(4). The Central Government may, from time to time, specify, by notification, the goods whose import shall be prohibited under this paragraph... The procedure for conducting an enquiry by the Director General of Foreign Trade into the use of forced labour in the production of such goods shall be as prescribed in the Handbook of Procedures, 2023." New Para 11.64 defines "Forced Labour" per ILO Convention No. 29. EFFECTIVE DATE, still an inference: the text ties effect to "the expiry of 30 days from the date of publication of this Notification in the Official Gazette," and no source -- egazette.gov.in, PIB or press -- states a Gazette publication date distinct from DGFT's own notification date (13/07/2026) and portal posting (14/07/2026). THE INFERRED EFFECTIVE DATE PASSED ON AUGUST 12, 2026 AND NOTHING CONFIRMS IT: as of August 19, seven days past the inferred date, no source reports that the prohibition has taken effect, and the Gazette publication date remains unstated everywhere checked (egazette.gov.in, PIB, Indian press, Hindi-language search). Source: DGFT Notification No. 23/2026-27 (primary document); DGFT notification index, dgft.gov.in (checked directly August 10, 2026); corroborated by Taxscan, Business Today, The Wire and an ELP legal alert.

Summary and Source: MATERIAL ADVANCE THIS RUN, VERIFIED AGAINST THE HEBREW SOURCE DIRECTLY: the KNESSET ECONOMIC COMMITTEE (Va'adat HaKalkala) has UNANIMOUSLY APPROVED the order banning imports of goods made with forced labour. JDN's report, read directly in Hebrew, states: "Va'adat HaKalkala shel HaKnesset ishra hayom (hamishi) pe echad tzav histori ha'oser larishona al yevu mutzarim she'yutzru be'avodat kfiya" -- the Knesset Economic Committee approved today (Thursday), unanimously, a historic order prohibiting for the first time the import of products produced with forced labour. DATE PINNED DOWN HERE, which the research pass could not do: the article says "today (Thursday)" and carries the Hebrew date byline 30 Av, and 30 Av 5786 corresponds to THURSDAY, AUGUST 13, 2026 -- the weekday and the Hebrew date agree, so the committee approval is dated August 13, 2026. The order was initiated by the Ministry of Economy following staff work coordinated by Prof. Avi Simhon of the National Economic Council, and the report is explicit that it was taken under the shadow of the US tariff, framed as aligning Israel with international standards and enabling an approach to Washington to reduce the tariff on Israeli exports to 10%. STRUCTURE, which is why this is not yet Yes: the order is expressly a framework -- "a foundational legal infrastructure" that will now ALLOW concrete products to be added to the prohibited-import list. Every future addition of specific products will require FRESH approval of the Economic Committee, accompanied by scrutiny of objection and appeal mechanisms and by adequate preparation periods for importers before any prohibition takes effect. So no product is banned yet, and no signed ministerial order or Reshumot (official gazette) entry has been reported. CLASSIFICATION STAYS PARTIAL on that basis -- committee approval of an order is a decisive step but not yet an issued instrument. FORWARD-LOOKING NOTE for future runs: once the order is signed and published in Reshumot, Israel should move to YES even with an empty product schedule, on the same reasoning that treats Trinidad and Tobago's Customs Act s.45(1)(w) and India's FTP Para 2.20B as Yes despite their designation-dependent structure. The Cabinet decision of July 26, 2026 (Hebrew sources Walla and Davar) remains the origin of the process, and follow-up Hebrew searching this run corroborates that it set an explicit 90-DAY implementation window -- directing Economy Minister Nir Barkat to stand up the order together with its mechanism design, appeals and reporting arrangements -- which places the outer deadline around late October 2026 and is consistent with the August 13 committee approval landing well inside it. Re-checked August 19, 2026 in Hebrew: still no signed ministerial order and no Reshumot entry, six days after the committee approval. FALSE-DATE GUARD, still standing: a claim that the decision was "approved February 22, 2026" has surfaced on numerous runs and has never been corroborated in any language; it is not adopted. Source: JDN (Hebrew), August 13, 2026, read directly; Emess (Hebrew); Walla and Davar (Hebrew), July 2026.

Summary and Source: Peru's forced-labour import-ban bill was formally submitted to Congress on July 2, 2026 with "very urgent" status requested and referred to the Foreign Trade and Economy committees on July 6, but was never taken up: the Foreign Trade Commission closed its 2025-2026 session without addressing it and the Permanent Commission's term ended July 15. The new bicameral Congress (2026-2031) was seated July 28, 2026 and the bill remains unassigned. On the Executive's parallel route, Foreign Trade and Tourism Minister Rogers Valencia said a forced-labour import/dealings prohibition would be folded into the government's request to Congress for delegated legislative powers ("facultades legislativas"). PRECISION CORRECTION this run: this row previously stated that the Council of Ministers did not approve that request at its August 5 session. That overstated the sourcing. What the sources actually support is that the session was postponed from August 2 -- when the government said the "conditions do not exist" for approval and the proposal was still being refined at technical level -- and was rescheduled to August 5; no source reports the OUTCOME of the August 5 session. Re-checked in Spanish on August 15, 2026, including the official gazette elperuano.pe: the outcome of the August 5 session is STILL unreported by any source TEN DAYS later, and no Decreto Legislativo or Ley on forced-labour imports has been published -- renewed Spanish-language searching returns only the August 3 La Republica item confirming the session was scheduled, and an August 10 opinion column on delegated legislative powers generally, neither of which states whether the request was approved or reached Congress. FURTHER DETAIL THIS RUN, recorded with its tension flagged: Caretas reported on July 29, 2026 that the Executive was seeking delegated powers for 120 days across security, MYPEs, employment, formalisation, productive development, the tax regime, customs and trade facilitation -- but that report does NOT mention a forced-labour provision among the listed matters. Whether the forced-labour prohibition survived into the text actually put before Congress is therefore unconfirmed; it rests on Mincetur's separate statement of intent. Note also the apparent sequencing tension: that report predates the August 2 postponement and the August 5 session, so it is not treated here as evidence that the request has cleared the Council of Ministers. Re-checked August 19, 2026: the August 5 outcome remains unreported by any source FOURTEEN DAYS on. (A research pass this run put the gap at sixteen days; the arithmetic is wrong -- August 5 to August 19 is fourteen days -- and the row uses the correct figure.) NEW NEGATIVE CHECK, at the register rather than through news: congreso.gob.pe was searched directly and NO project number has been assigned to any delegated-powers or forced-labour bill, so there is still no evidence the request has been formally received by Congress. GAZETTE CHECKED AT THE DAY LEVEL this run: the El Peruano legal-norms digests for both August 5 and August 15, 2026 were examined and contain no Decreto Legislativo, Ley or delegated-powers instrument touching forced labour -- only routine ministerial and supreme resolutions. ONE CLAIM RECORDED BUT NOT ADOPTED: a search-engine synthesis of the August reporting asserts that the forced-labour import/dealings prohibition WAS included in the delegated-powers request discussed on August 5, which would resolve the open question of whether the clause survived into the submitted text. That synthesis is not a named, dated article and could not be traced to a primary source, and this row has been burned before by asserting more than the sources support, so the inclusion question stays OPEN rather than resolved. It rests, as before, only on Mincetur's separate statement of intent, and no Decreto Legislativo or Ley on forced-labour imports has been published. No approval, no confirmed submission carrying the forced-labour clause and no published measure through either route, so the classification is unchanged, and the row continues not to assert a negative decision that was never actually reported. Source: Congreso del Peru communications; Gestion, Infobae and Caretas, August 2-3, 2026; La Republica, August 3, 2026; RPP Noticias, July 24, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (bill formally submitted to Congress July 2, 2026 and referred to committee July 6, never taken up and still unassigned in the new bicameral Congress; the Executive's parallel delegated-legislative-powers request, which would carry a forced-labour import prohibition, was postponed from August 2 to August 5 and its outcome has not been reported -- no approval, no confirmed submission carrying the forced-labour clause and no published measure as of August 20, 2026. El Comercio, August 19, 2026 now reports the outcome directly: the delegated-powers request has NOT been approved after FOUR Council of Ministers sessions -- July 29 and August 5, 12 and 14 -- and the August 5 session did not revisit the topic at all; the six areas listed in the request make no mention of forced labour, no project number assigned in congreso.gob.pe and the El Peruano digests for August 5 and 15 containing no forced-labour instrument)

Summary and Source: Switzerland disputes USTR's findings, maintaining that existing constitutional, civil and criminal law suffices; swissinfo.ch notes that unlike the EU, Switzerland has no legislation explicitly prohibiting forced-labour imports, which is the stated basis for its higher tier, and that a draft due-diligence law would reach only around 30 large companies rather than banning imports. New this run: Switzerland concluded a broader US trade agreement lowering its general tariff to about 15% in exchange for roughly $200bn of US investment through 2028. Checked specifically for a forced-labour or Section 307 clause per the Jordan precedent -- this is a general tariff-and-investment deal with no forced-labour import-prohibition commitment found, so it does not place Switzerland on the RTA-commitment watchlist. CLARIFIED AUGUST 13, 2026: the underlying November 2025 US-Switzerland-Liechtenstein instrument is a NON-BINDING joint framework statement / letter of intent, not a signed agreement; it references cooperation on forced-labour issues in general terms but contains no import-prohibition clause, and no final signed bilateral agreement text exists. So there is no treaty-level commitment capable of putting Switzerland on the watchlist even on the Jordan reading. Source: swissinfo.ch, July 24, 2026; Barchart/Reuters, July 2026.

Summary and Source: Taiwan's 10%-tier eligibility rests on its February 12, 2026 US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, under which Taiwan committed to prohibit forced-labor-produced imports. INSTRUMENT NOW ISSUED: on July 30, 2026 the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Ministry of Labor jointly issued the "Operating Guidelines for Restricting the Import of Forced Labor Goods" and a companion "Review Committee Establishment Guidelines," under Article 11 of the Foreign Trade Act -- the administrative instrument previously recorded here as forthcoming. A 12-member review committee co-chaired by the MOEA and MOL ministers must decide within 30 days of receiving a forced-labour referral, after which the competent authority publishes a notice restricting or lifting the import restriction, with Customs and the Finance Ministry notifying importers to return or destroy listed goods. Column 6 accordingly upgraded to Taiwan's own Ministry of Labor announcement. Classification remains Partial on the same reasoning applied to the Philippines' Joint Administrative Order: this is an enforcement regime under existing statutory authority, not a standalone enacted import prohibition, and no Legislative Yuan bill has been tabled (the separate Employment Service Act amendments address labour brokerage, not imports). SEQUENCE CLARIFIED this run: the Executive Yuan approved the mechanism on July 29, 2026 and MOEA/MOL formally announced it the following day, July 30 -- the date this row already carried. Also new: Amnesty International Taiwan is publicly pressing the government to LEGISLATE the labour provisions of the US-Taiwan agreement rather than continue relying on administrative guidelines, which is the step that would move Taiwan from Partial to Yes; no Legislative Yuan bill has been tabled. Source: Public Television Service (PTS) and Executive Yuan Section 301 portal, July 29-30, 2026; Amnesty International Taiwan; Ministry of Labor (Taiwan, official), July 30, 2026; Newtalk and Taipei Times, July 30-31, 2026; USTR fact sheet, February 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (US-Taiwan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, February 12, 2026 treaty commitment, now implemented through MOEA/MOL Operating Guidelines and a Review Committee issued July 30, 2026 under Foreign Trade Act Art. 11; still an administrative regime under existing authority -- no statutory import prohibition enacted and no Legislative Yuan bill tabled)

A measure being drafted is not a measure formally tabled or published, so it falls short of the Partial threshold; if the bill is actually tabled, Thailand moves to Partial. Summary and Source: The specific domestic instrument has now been located and verified directly: Trinidad and Tobago's Finance Act, 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), assented to on 25 June 2026 and published in Legal Supplement Part A to the Trinidad and Tobago Gazette, Vol. 65, No. 111, 29 June 2026, section 24 amends the Customs Act (Chap. 78:01) section 45(1) by inserting a new paragraph: "(w) all goods produced from forced labour as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade". Section 45(1) is the Customs Act's list of prohibited/restricted imports, so this is a genuine, enacted, gazetted forced-labor import prohibition (designation-dependent -- the specific list of goods is left to the Minister with responsibility for trade to designate, similar in structure to several other economies' framework-style bans). This confirms and supersedes the prior entry's reliance on USTR's Federal Register final-action notice (which had stated, without naming the instrument, that Trinidad and Tobago "adopt[ed] a forced labor import prohibition subsequent to the publication of the June 5, 2026 FRN" -- the Finance Act's 25 June 2026 assent date fits neatly within that window). USTR's final action (July 23, 2026) placed Trinidad and Tobago in the 10% tariff tier on this basis. Source: Trinidad and Tobago e-Gazette (printery.gov.tt), Finance Act 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), 29 June 2026; USTR Federal Register final-action notice, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Finance Act, 2026, Act No. 16 of 2026, assented 25 June 2026, gazetted 29 June 2026, section 24 amends Customs Act Chap. 78:01 s.45(1) by adding paragraph (w) prohibiting the importation of goods produced from forced labour, as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade -- a framework-style ban pending ministerial designation of the specific goods list)

Summary and Source: Vietnam's Government issued Decree No. 292/2026/ND-CP on July 22, 2026, implementing the Law on Foreign Trade Management; item 23 of its Appendix I prohibited-import list bans "products and goods extracted, produced, or manufactured wholly or partly through forced labor." Effective September 5, 2026 (45 days after issuance). Vietnam's Foreign Ministry separately rejected USTR's findings and reiterated that Vietnam "strictly prohibits all forms of forced labour." IMPLEMENTATION MECHANISM PINNED DOWN this run: per Article 5(2) of the decree, ministries and ministerial-level agencies are tasked with announcing the detailed HS-code-level goods lists built on Appendix I -- so the decree is self-executing as a prohibition but depends on those ministerial lists for operational scope. Re-checked in Vietnamese on August 20, 2026, sixteen days before the decree bites: no ministerial HS-code list, no implementing circular (thong tu) and no General Department of Customs preparation notice has been published. WATCH ITEM NOW RESOLVED: yesterday's single-source claim that the forced-labour category is administered by the Ministry of Interior/Home Affairs (Bo Noi vu) rather than a trade ministry has been corroborated by multiple independent Vietnamese sources (luatvietnam.vn, congluan.vn, vietnam.vn) citing Appendix I of the decree directly ("nhom hang hoa nay do Bo Noi vu quan ly"). It is therefore adopted rather than merely flagged. This matters practically: it identifies which body must issue the Article 5(2) HS-code list, and it is an unusual assignment for an import-control category, so the list is not to be expected from the trade ministry. Note the decree predated USTR's July 23 final determination by one day yet Vietnam was still placed in the 12.5% tier. Source: Bao Chinh Phu (Vietnam Government Portal), July 22-23, 2026; Lao Dong; LuatVietnam and RBV, July-August 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Decree No. 292/2026/ND-CP, issued July 22, 2026, Appendix I item 23; effective September 5, 2026, with the ministerial HS-code goods lists required by Article 5(2), any implementing circular, and customs preparation notices all still unpublished as of August 20, sixteen days before the effective date; the goods category is administered by the Ministry of Interior (Bo Noi vu) per Appendix I, corroborated across multiple Vietnamese sources)
